Standard SOAP Note Formats

Section 01 · LO 1

Why We Document, and the Essential Components of Every SOAP Note

Documentation is how a single patient encounter becomes something the rest of the care team — and your future self — can act on. It is also a legal document, a billing/coding document, and the raw material that populates the EHR (Epic runs more than half of U.S. sites).

🗂️
Why physicians document: to communicate what happened in the encounter; to share information across the care team over time (physicians, consultants, staff); to give SOAP notes their organizational framework for clinical reasoning and medical decision-making; because notes are legal documents that protect you (or expose you and your team) if written poorly; to support billing and coding; and because notes feed directly into the EHR/EMR — a federally required, nationwide record-keeping system.

What Shapes How a Note Is Written ⭐ HY

Documentation format is not one-size-fits-all. Four factors change what a note looks like:

1 · Where

SettingOutpatient/ambulatory clinic, in-patient/hospital, urgent outpatient or ER, or a procedure/surgery center — each has different documentation norms.

2 · Who

DocumenterPrimary care or resident physician, consulting specialist, mid-level (PA/RNP), professional staff (RN/MA), or a medical student — scope and depth differ.

3 · New vs. Known

Patient statusA new patient needs a full history; a known patient returning for follow-up needs a review and update of existing history.

4 · Visit Type

TypeAcute, chronic, multiple problems, progress/follow-up, annual PE, consult, pre-operative, or pregnancy & delivery.

The Four Letters, in One Line Each

S — Subjective

What the patient says or reports, in common language/non-medical jargon.

O — Objective

Data: vitals, general appearance, exam findings, and reports you measure or review — stated in medical jargon.

A — Assessment

Your analysis and explanation of the chief complaint from the HPI/PMHx/ROS/vitals/PE/reports: a primary diagnosis with ≥3 differentials (most → least likely, but cannot rule out), plus the Somatic Dysfunction region if an OSE was done.

P — Plan

How you'll evaluate, manage/treat, and advance care — Diagnostics, Therapeutics, OMM/OMT, Patient Education, Follow-Up, and checking Understanding/Agreement.
⚠️
Graded, every time: All information must sit under the correct category — Subjective vs. Objective vs. Assessment vs. Plan. Content that's clinically correct but filed under the wrong letter still loses points. Labels must be used for S/O/A/P and every subcategory within them, and the note has to be organized and easy to read.
Practice Question
A patient tells you her sore throat is a 7/10 and started 3 days ago. Where does this belong in the note?
A. Objective, under Vitals
B. Subjective, within the HPI (Severity and Timing of LOPPQRSTA)
C. Assessment, as a differential
D. Plan, under Patient Education
Answer: B. Anything the patient tells you — including a pain scale and duration — is Subjective and belongs in the HPI, captured by the LOPPQRSTA elements Severity and Timing.
Section 02 · LO 2

Subjective — What the Patient Says

Label it Subjective or S, then document Patient Name, Age, and DOB (deidentified in Student OMM Clinic or any real clinical setting).

Chief Complaint (CC) & History of Present Illness (HPI)

CC is separated out; HPI is a lead-in sentence plus a short paragraph
HPI intro template"This (or name) is a __ y/o, (gender or birth sex, noting sex as it relates to exogenous/endogenous hormone exposure where relevant to risk — e.g. testosterone → elevated Hgb/liver enzymes; estrogen/progesterone → thrombotic risk), who presents with __."
Acute"__ days of __ (symptom/problem)."
Subacute/chronic"__ months/years of this problem," or "was in usual state of [good/poor] health until __ when he/she developed __."
Also askHas this CC occurred before? Was trauma related to the problem?
🧠
LOPPQRSTA — use it to guarantee HPI completeness: Location, Onset, Provocation, Palliation, Quality, Radiation, Severity, Timing, Associated symptoms.
🧠
ICEE — listen for or ask about, then repeat back to the patient: Ideas (what the patient thinks is wrong), Concerns (what brought them in), Effects (impact on their life), Expectations (for the visit). Rubric: must list ≥3 for full credit, ≥2 for partial.

The Rest of the History ⭐ HY

PMHx

Chronic diagnoses (what + when diagnosed), previous hospitalizations (why + when), immunizations (up to date?), pertinent testing/specialty consults.

PSHx

Procedures/surgeries — what, when, and why if not apparent.

Allergies

Medications (with reactions — rash vs. anaphylaxis/swelling/breathing difficulty), OTC/supplements, foods (e.g. peanuts), and environmental (pollen, bee stings).

Meds

Prescribed and OTC/herbal/supplements — what, dose, frequency, and how the patient actually takes them.

FHx

Parents and siblings: health issues, cancer, age, cause of death if deceased. Include grandparents/children if genetically relevant. Ethnicity may confer genetic risk and, when relevant, is listed here rather than in the CC/one-liner.

SocHx

Occupation (current/past + exposures), living situation/support/safety at home, travel, Tobacco/Vaping/ETOH/other substances (how much, how long, quit?), diet, exercise, sexuality/reproductive history, hobbies, race (patient's own chosen language), religion/spirituality, disability, military service, culture, gender-related topics, financial status, advance directives, and other social determinants of health.

Review of Systems (ROS)

Document positives together, then negatives together, per system, using phrases/lists and appropriate abbreviations:

💬
"General ROS was positive for fever, weight loss, night sweats, and fatigue, and negative for chills, weakness, or changes in sleep." "Pulmonary: +SOB, DOE; yet − for cough and wheezing."
  • 7 General ROS required (F, Fatigue, Sleep disturbance, Chills, Weight loss/gain, Weakness, Night sweats, etc.) — ≥4 needed for partial credit.
  • 3 best systems related to the CC, ≥3 questions each — ≥3 systems needed for full credit, ≥2 for partial.
  • Positive ROS elements must be clearly grouped together by system; negative elements grouped together by system.
  • A detailed/complicated positive ROS can occasionally be written in full sentences; ROS-related findings tied tightly to the CC may also live in the HPI as Associated Symptoms.
Practice Question
Per the OCS 2 rubric, how many ICEE elements must be documented to receive full ("Yes") credit?
A. 1
B. 2
C. 3
D. All 4
Answer: C. At least 3 of the 4 ICEE elements (Ideas, Concerns, Effects, Expectations) are required for full ("Yes") credit; 2 elements earns Partial.
Section 03 · LO 3

Objective — What You Examine or Receive

Label it Objective or O. Order in a complete exam is usually head-to-toe after vitals and general appearance.

Vitals

Temp, Heart Rate, Resp Rate, and BP individually reported — all 4 required for full credit, ≥2 for partial. Add O2 Sat, Height, Weight, BMI when relevant.

General Appearance

What the patient looks like and how they're acting/sitting — e.g. "alert, in no distress, conversational and well dressed" or "anxious and tearful." Never document "A&O x3" unless you actually tested person/place/time.

System Exam Documentation Examples ⭐ HY

Cranial Nerve / Neuro

Example"CN 2–12 intact BL," plus any special tests with +/− findings. Don't claim a CN is intact if not examined (most physicians skip CN1/olfaction unless it's a problem). For DTRs/dermatomes/myotomes, list strength 0–5/5 and reflex 0–4/4 for each one tested, bilaterally.

HEENT

ExampleNormocephalic without lesions/scars/rashes; normal red reflex; PERRLA BL; TMs intact with + cone of light BL; nasal mucosa moist without erythema/polyps/discharge; oral mucosa moist, dentition intact; no lymphadenopathy or thyromegaly.

Cardiac

Example"RRR with S1/S2 and without M/G/R" or the abnormal finding, e.g. "systolic murmur best heard at right sternal border."

Pulmonary

Example"CTA BL" without R/R/W, or "diffuse expiratory wheezing" if present.

Abdomen

ExampleAlways look → listen → percuss/palpate. "+BS x 4 quadrants" and "positive rebound pain in the RUQ to deep palpation" if present.

Musculoskeletal

ExampleVisual exam, AROM, PROM, and Strength of affected joints — always in bilateral comparison — plus special tests with +/− findings.
🎯
Three PE traps to avoid:
1) Too general — "Neuro: Dermatomes, Myotomes, DTRs intact" says nothing useful.
2) Missing detail — which extremity? What laterality? (L1 dermatome is tested over clothing/drape — the only exception — so document it that way.)
3) False documentation — never write a finding you didn't actually elicit (e.g. claiming CN1 intact, or a DTR of +2/4 when it was really +1/4).
Better: "Dermatomes L2–S2 on skin intact BL, L1 intact BL over the drape; Myotomes LE intact BL; DTRs Patellar & Achilles +2/4 BL."

Data: Labs, Radiology, Reports

RuleDocument ALL previous labs/x-rays/reports with actual specific values — never as "negative" or "normal." In-patient notes focus on the past 24 hours and new changes from prior labs. In Geriatrics, MiniCog/PHQ-2/PHQ-9/MoCA scores and interpretations are Objective findings, placed at the end of this section.
📎
Worked example (Objective, sore throat visit): "Vitals: T 102.2F, HR 104, RR 18, BP 140/90, SaO2 98% RA. General: stated age, mild distress, alert, conversational, irritated from waiting. HEENT: PERRLA, no conjunctival injection, EOMI BL; TMs intact + cone of light BL; nasal mucosa moist, no erythema/discharge/polyps BL; OP + white exudate on BL tonsils, enlarged with erythema and cobblestoning; lymph nodes mobile BL, rubbery, enlarged sublingual/anterior/posterior cervical chain < 1 cm BL; thyroid not enlarged. Cardiac: no carotid bruits BL, RRR with S1S2, no M/G/R. Pulmonary: CTA BL, no adventitial sounds, egophony/whispered pectoriloquy negative, resonant percussion BL. OSE: OA FSrRl, AA Rr, Cervical Spine C4 FSRr, with myofascial TART changes in the suboccipital area BL."
Section 04 · LO 4

Assessment — Primary Problem, Differentials, and Somatic Dysfunction

Label it Assessment or A. This is your analysis and explanation of the CC, built from the HPI, PMHx, ROS, vitals, PE, and any reports.

Template

1. Primary Problem"The Primary Problem for this patient is: ____."
2. Differential Diagnoses (≥3)A) Most likely DDx, because [defend with Hx/PE/testing]. B) 2nd most likely, because [defend]. C) 3rd — either your least-likely-but-can't-rule-out DDx, or something less likely that you defend as less likely and why.
3. Somatic DysfunctionDocumented by region, translated from OSE findings.
4. Secondary/tertiary problemsIf present — may or may not need their own plan; if unrelated to the primary complaint they get a full 6-prong plan of their own.

Worked Example — DDx for "Sore Throat" ⭐ HY

DiagnosisLikelihoodRationale (Defense)
Strep PharyngitisMost likely + White exudate, fever of 102.2°F, anterior & posterior cervical lymphadenopathy on exam, and contact with a +Strep person
Viral SyndromeLess likely Also has + white exudate and +Strep contact, which argue against a purely viral picture
Seasonal AllergiesLess likely No history of allergies; allergies don't cause white exudate or fever
Throat CancerLeast likely (can't-miss) No history of smoking/vaping/nicotine use; rubbery lymph nodes ≤1 cm; acute symptoms with fever argue against malignancy
🔬
Diagnoses differ by History + Symptoms + PE findings, not by CC alone. Strep pharyngitis classically shows patchy white/yellow exudate on erythematous, swollen tonsils; viral pharyngitis more often shows diffuse erythema of the posterior pharynx without exudate. The exam finding — not just "sore throat" — is what separates the differentials.

How to Build a Differential Diagnosis

Systems-BasedNEURO, HEENT, PSYCH, HEME/ONC, CARDIO, PULM, DERM, ID, RENAL, GI, GU, ENDO, REPRO, MSK, etc.
VINDICATEVascular, Infection, Neoplasm, Drugs, Inflammatory, Idiopathic, Congenital, Autoimmune, Trauma, Endocrine/Metabolic.
Look-It-UpStart from one hypothesis; your reference text's differential section does the rest.
AnatomicAsk what tissue lives in the region of the complaint.
📝
Worksheet approach: list concerning findings from History and from the Physical side by side → identify the critical, can't-miss diagnoses at this point → ask what the OSE told you → identify which diagnoses are consistent with all your findings.

Somatic Dysfunction (SD)

  • SD is documented in the Assessment by region — used for billing and coding.
  • 10 possible regions: head, neck, thoracic, ribs, lumbar, sacrum, pelvis, abdomen (and other, e.g. lymphatic), upper extremity, lower extremity.
  • Translation example: OSE finding "T5 ERSr" → Assessment: "Somatic Dysfunction of the Thoracic Spine."
📎
Worked example (Assessment, sore throat visit): "1) Primary Dx: Sore Throat. DDx 1: Strep Pharyngitis... DDx 2: Viral Syndrome... DDx 3: Seasonal Allergies... DDx 4: Throat Cancer... 2) Somatic Dysfunction(s): Head and Cervical Spine, based on OSE. 3) Other Diagnoses: Elevated Blood Pressure — DDx 1: BP 140/90 likely due to illness/fever; DDx 2: stress/white-coat; DDx 3: inaccurate reading, caffeine, new idiopathic HTN, or FHx of HTN."
Practice Question
An OSE reveals T5 is extended, rotated, and side-bent right (T5 ERSr) with myofascial TART changes. How should this be written in the Assessment?
A. "T5 ERSr" (copy the OSE notation directly into Assessment)
B. "Somatic Dysfunction of the Thoracic Spine"
C. Leave it out of Assessment; it only belongs in Objective
D. "Thoracic vertebral subluxation"
Answer: B. OSE findings (boney/myofascial TART, laterality) live in Objective; the Assessment translates them into a Somatic Dysfunction diagnosis by region, since regions are what's used for billing and coding.
Section 05 · Bridges LO 3–LO 5

The OSE → Somatic Dysfunction → OMT Documentation Chain

The Osteopathic Structural Exam threads through all three later sections of the note. Losing track of this chain is one of the most common ways points are lost.

Step 1 · Objective
List OSE findings by body region (head, neck, thorax, ribs, lumbar, sacrum, pelvis, abdomen, UE, LE) — boney and myofascial TART findings, with laterality. No diagnosis language here yet.
Step 2 · Assessment
Translate the OSE findings into a Somatic Dysfunction diagnosis, named by region (not by the raw OSE notation).
Step 3 · Plan
State the OMT technique(s) you'll use for that SD at the next visit — or, if you treated the same day, write a full OMT Procedure Note (technique, consent, and how the patient tolerated it).
✅
Good example (from lecture): OSE: "OA FSrRl, AA Rr, Cervical Spine C4 FSRr, with myofascial TART changes in the suboccipital area BL." → Assessment: "Somatic Dysfunctions of the Head and Cervical Spine." → OMT Plan: "MFR, ST, and FPR to SD of the Head and Cervical Spine next visit."
⚠️
You will lose points if: OSE findings are documented in Objective but never translated to a Somatic Dysfunction region in Assessment — OR — a Somatic Dysfunction is diagnosed but no OMT technique is listed in the Plan for the next visit.
💡
If you forgot a step: say so. If you forgot to do the OSE, or the SD assessment, or the OMT plan, state that you'll re-evaluate/perform it at the next visit — partial credit is available for an honest plan to catch up, never for fabricating a finding you didn't actually obtain.
Section 06 · LO 5

Plan — Six Prongs

Label it Plan or P. This is how you'll evaluate, treat, and educate the patient for each numbered problem in the Assessment. Each additional, unrelated problem needs its own 6-prong plan.

1 · Diagnostics

Tests you'll order and why — imaging, labs, EKG, specialty/surgical consults, Psych, Social Work.

2 · Therapeutics

Meds (be specific — a drug or class, not just "an antibiotic"), splints/casts, PT/OT/Speech, referrals to Cardiology/Surgery/Psychiatry/Social Services.

3 · OMT

Techniques planned for the SD next visit, OR the full OMT Procedure Note if performed same-day (consent, technique, tolerance).

4 · Patient Education

What you explained (or will explain) about labs, meds, diet/exercise, immunizations, OMT, RICE, or preventative health.

5 · Follow-Up

Specific timing and mode — office visit, phone, telehealth, or "go to the ER if ___."

6 · Understanding & Agreement

Does the patient agree to the plan? If not, why not (language, travel, cost, side effects — SDOH). Always ask if the patient has questions.
📎
Worked example (Plan, sore throat visit): "1) Diagnostics: Rapid Strep Screen, Throat Culture if negative, CBC w/ Diff, consider Monospot. 2) Therapeutics: If Strep+, Penicillin or Amoxicillin per age/weight × 10 days (alternate antibiotic if PCN-allergic); OTC Acetaminophen and/or Ibuprofen per age/weight for pain. 3) OMT: Thoracic Inlet MFR for drainage, Cervical ST, and FPR to OA/AA/Cervical due to SD of Head & Cervical Spine, next visit. 4) Patient Education: screening/culture process, bacterial vs. viral infection, medications, warm salt-water gargle, hot chicken soup, no work until 24h+ on antibiotics, work note, PCN/Ibuprofen side effects and dosing. 5) Follow-Up: ER if unable to swallow saliva or symptoms worsen; otherwise call/FU as needed. 6) Patient understands and agrees to the plan; no further questions."
  • If there's genuinely nothing to add for a prong, document it explicitly: "No Tx indicated," or "No plans for Diagnostics. No Therapeutics or supportive care needed."
  • A second, unrelated problem (e.g. ongoing tobacco use) needs its own 6-prong plan — though some prongs can be dropped if truly not applicable (e.g. no OSE needed for a nicotine-use plan; Follow-Up may be shared with Problem 1 rather than repeated).
  • In Student OMM Clinic, print your name, sign the note, and note your level (e.g. OMS 2) and the date.
Practice Question
A patient has a somatic dysfunction of the lumbar spine documented in the Assessment, but you plan no OMT this visit and want to treat it next time. What must the Plan include?
A. Nothing — OMT can be skipped since it wasn't done today
B. The specific OMT technique(s) you'll perform on the lumbar SD at the next visit
C. A note that the somatic dysfunction has resolved
D. A referral to Physical Therapy instead
Answer: B. Any documented Somatic Dysfunction requires a corresponding OMT plan — either a same-day procedure note, or named techniques planned for the next visit. Leaving it out costs points even if the SD itself was documented correctly.
Section 07 · Demonstrates LO 1–5

Full Worked Example — Acute Sore Throat Visit

The complete note, assembled section-by-section from Dr. Doane's lecture examples, showing how S/O/A/P and OSE→SD→OMT fit together in one acute visit.

Click to expand the full SOAP note
Subjective

CC: Sore throat, acute. HPI: "This patient is a __ y/o who presents with 3 days of sore throat, worsening, 7/10 severity, associated with fever and difficulty swallowing; denies cough..." (LOPPQRSTA elements embedded). ICEE: patient is worried this is strep and wants antibiotics; concerned about missing work; expects testing and treatment today.

Objective

Vitals: T 102.2°F, HR 104, RR 18, BP 140/90, SaO2 98% RA. General: stated age, mild distress, alert, conversational, irritated from waiting. HEENT: PERRLA, no conjunctival injection, EOMI BL; TMs intact + cone of light BL; nasal mucosa moist, no erythema/discharge/polyps BL; OP + white exudate on BL tonsils, enlarged with erythema and cobblestoning; tongue without defects; lymph nodes mobile BL, rubbery, enlarged sublingual/anterior/posterior cervical chain nodes < 1 cm BL; no thyromegaly. Cardiac: no carotid bruits BL, RRR with S1S2, no M/G/R. Pulmonary: CTA BL, no adventitial sounds, egophony/whispered pectoriloquy negative, percussion resonant BL. OSE: OA FSrRl, AA Rr, Cervical Spine C4 FSRr, with myofascial TART changes in the suboccipital area BL.

Assessment

1) Primary Dx: Sore Throat. DDx 1: Strep Pharyngitis (most likely — + white exudate, fever 102.2°F, cervical lymphadenopathy, +Strep contact). DDx 2: Viral Syndrome (less likely — exudate + Strep contact argue against). DDx 3: Seasonal Allergies (less likely — no allergy history; allergies don't cause exudate/fever). DDx 4: Throat Cancer (least likely — no smoking history, rubbery nodes ≤1 cm, acute course with fever). 2) Somatic Dysfunction(s): Head and Cervical Spine, based on OSE. 3) Other Diagnoses: Elevated Blood Pressure (BP 140/90) — differentials include acute illness/fever, stress/white-coat, inaccurate reading/caffeine, or new/idiopathic HTN.

Plan

1) Diagnostics: Rapid Strep Screen; Throat Culture & C&S if negative; CBC w/ Diff; consider Monospot. 2) Therapeutics: If Strep+, Penicillin or Amoxicillin per age/weight × 10 days (alternate antibiotic if PCN-allergic); OTC Acetaminophen and/or Ibuprofen per age/weight for pain. 3) OMT: Thoracic Inlet MFR for drainage, Cervical Soft Tissue, and FPR to OA/AA/Cervical, due to SD of Head & Cervical Spine, next visit. 4) Patient Education: screening/culture process, bacterial vs. viral infection, medication and side-effect counseling, warm salt-water gargle, hot chicken soup, no work until 24h+ on antibiotics, work note. 5) Follow-Up: go to the ER if unable to swallow saliva or symptoms worsen; otherwise call/follow up as needed if not improving. 6) Patient understands and agrees to the plan; no further questions.

Section 08 · Supports Every LO

Grading Rubric & Approved Abbreviations

The Acute SOAP Note Grading Rubric checks each component as Yes / Partial / No. Knowing the thresholds ahead of time is the difference between a full-credit note and one that's "close but incomplete."

Rubric Quick-Check ⭐ HY

SectionItemThreshold for Full ("Yes") Credit
SubjectiveICEEList ≥3 of 4 elements (2 = Partial)
SubjectiveGeneral ROSAll 7 general ROS items (≥4 = Partial)
SubjectiveSystem ROS3 best systems, positives & negatives grouped (2 systems = Partial)
ObjectiveVitalsAll 4 (Temp/HR/RR/BP) individually listed (≥2 = Partial)
ObjectivePE systems≥2 best systems documented with elements, abnormalities, and laterality
ObjectiveSpecial tests≥3 best special tests, including positives and laterality (2 = Partial)
AssessmentDifferentials≥3 DDx with plausible rationale under the Primary Problem (2 = Partial)
AssessmentSomatic DysfunctionLinked to positive OSE findings; written correctly as an SD Region
PlanAll 6 prongsDiagnostics, Therapeutics, OMT, Pt. Education, Follow-Up, Understanding/Agreement all present
OverallOrganizationCorrect category for every line; S/O/A/P and subcategory labels used; no false documentation

A far larger reference (300+ terms) is available in the Madison Memorial Hospital abbreviation list and the full NBOME abbreviations list — use those as lookup references; this table covers the set most directly useful for a standard acute OCS 2 note.

Section 09 · Final Recap

Rapid Review

S / O / A / PWhat patient says → what you measure/examine → your analysis (primary + ≥3 DDx + SD) → your evaluation/treatment plan.
LOPPQRSTALocation, Onset, Provocation, Palliation, Quality, Radiation, Severity, Timing, Associated symptoms.
ICEEIdeas, Concerns, Effects, Expectations — need ≥3 for full credit.
VINDICATEVascular, Infection, Neoplasm, Drugs, Inflammatory, Idiopathic, Congenital, Autoimmune, Trauma, Endocrine/Metabolic.
6-Prong PlanDiagnostics → Therapeutics → OMT → Patient Education → Follow-Up → Understanding & Agreement.
OSE ChainObjective (OSE findings, no dx) → Assessment (SD by region) → Plan (OMT technique next visit, or procedure note if same-day).
PE PitfallsDon't be too general; specify laterality/extent; never document a finding you didn't actually elicit.
Never Say "Normal"Labs/imaging/reports are documented with actual specific values, never as "normal" or "negative" alone.

⭐ SOAP Notes — High-Yield One-Pager

Condensed by topic cluster — SOAP Overview · Subjective · Objective · Assessment · Plan · OSE Chain · Grading Essentials

SOAP Overview

  • S: patient's own words, lay language
  • O: vitals, appearance, exam, reports — jargon OK
  • A: primary dx + ≥3 DDx (most→least likely, can't-rule-out) + SD region
  • P: Dx, Tx, OMT, Pt. Ed, F/U, Understanding/Agreement
  • Documentation shaped by: setting, documenter, new vs. known, visit type
  • Everything filed under the correct S/O/A/P label — misfiling loses points even if content is correct

Subjective

  • HPI intro: age/sex + LOPPQRSTA
  • ICEE ≥3/4 for full credit
  • PMHx/PSHx/Allergies/Meds/FHx/SocHx — each with specifics (what, when, dose, reaction)
  • ROS: 7 General required; 3 best systems ≥3 Qs each; positives/negatives grouped by system

Objective

  • Vitals: T/HR/RR/BP all 4 required
  • General appearance — describe, don't assume ("A&O x3" only if tested)
  • ≥2 systems w/ elements, abnormalities, laterality; ≥3 special tests
  • Never "normal/negative" alone — give the actual value
  • PE pitfalls: too general / missing laterality / false documentation

Assessment

  • Primary problem + ≥3 DDx, each defended by Hx/PE/testing
  • VINDICATE, systems-based, look-it-up, anatomic — 4 ways to build a DDx
  • SD documented by region (10 possible regions) — used for billing
  • Secondary/tertiary dx get their own DDx if relevant

Plan (6 Prongs)

  • Diagnostics — tests + why
  • Therapeutics — specific drug/class, referrals
  • OMT — technique for SD next visit, or procedure note if same-day
  • Patient Education, Follow-Up (specific timing/mode), Understanding & Agreement
  • "No Tx indicated" is a valid, explicit entry when nothing applies

OSE → SD → OMT Chain

  • Objective: OSE by region, TART + laterality, no dx yet
  • Assessment: translate to SD region (e.g. T5 ERSr → "SD of the Thoracic Spine")
  • Plan: name the OMT technique for that SD, or write the procedure note if done today
  • SD without an OMT plan = lost points; OSE without SD in Assessment = lost points
  • Forgot a step? Say you'll address it next visit — don't fabricate it

Master Rubric Quick-Check
